session_meta.research_objective:
Focus group guide exploring how men in the UK make everyday food
choices, how social context, work, hobbies, health, taste and other
people shape what they eat, how gender and masculinity may influence
food choices, and what would need to change for plant-based foods to
become more acceptable or appealing.
session_meta.topic_domain: Masculinity, food choice, animal product consumption, and plant-based eating
session_meta.participant_collective_identity: Men in the UK reflecting on food choices, male friendship, gender norms, and plant-based eating
session_meta.moderator_knowledge_brief:
Explore (1) everyday food decision-making, (2) the social contexts in
which men spend time with male friends, (3) the influence of other
people, work, hobbies, health, nutrition and taste on food choices,
(4) whether participants perceive gender as shaping what they eat,
(5) social acceptability and gendered meanings attached to vegetarian,
vegan, plant-based, feminine or masculine foods, and (6) what personal,
social and practical changes would make plant-based eating more viable
or appealing. The discussion should remain exploratory, non-judgmental,
and non-leading.

initial_session_plan.thematisation_approach: These participants will be framed as men in the UK reflecting on their own everyday lives — the places they go, the food they eat, the company they keep. The collective identity is grounded in the ordinary and the personal, not in any particular dietary position. I will position them as people whose honest, specific experiences are the entire point of the conversation, rather than as representatives of any group or perspective.
priority_research_areas: Gender and food choice (Section 3): High risk of socially desirable or abstract answers — 'I don't think gender affects me' is a common deflection. Needs behavioural grounding early and readiness to surface contradictions gently as they emerge in earlier sections.

Imagining a plant-based shift (Section 4): Risk of hypothetical/performative answers ('I'd need it to taste better') that lack personal specificity. Need to push toward real past moments — near-misses, experiments, meals that nearly worked — rather than general conditions.

Social acceptability and masculine/feminine food meanings: Likely to surface obliquely in Sections 1–3 before being addressed directly in Section 5. Requires tracking what is said about others' judgements, lads' settings, and food shame early, for use later.

Consensus risk across all main sections: Three men, similar age bracket and eating pattern (all meat-eaters, 50s), relatively homogeneous group — strong potential for rapid convergence on shared positions, especially on gender-not-affecting-choices and on plant-based resistance. Must monitor and invite dissent actively.

participant_notes.anticipated_role: Urban North West background may bring a slightly different cultural context to food and masculinity than the others. Age 53, meat-eater — likely comfortable speaking but profile gives no further differentiation signals. Monitor for whether he takes an early lead or waits.
Suburban South East — potentially different socioeconomic framing around food choices and plant-based availability. Age 50, meat-eater. No strong anticipation signals; profile is fairly neutral.

Rural/village East of England background is the most distinct in the group — may have different relationship to food sourcing, local produce, land, or food culture. Worth monitoring for whether rurality shapes his framing of plant-based foods differently. Age 52, meat-eater.
participant_notes.initial_attention_flag: Rural background may produce a qualitatively different perspective on plant-based eating — worth probing if he raises provenance, farming, or local food.

known_risk_conditions: Homogeneous group (three 50s-era British male meat-eaters) — high consensus risk on gender-doesn't-affect-me framing and on plant-based resistance. Plan invite_dissent moves proactively for Sections 3–5.

Topic may produce socially desirable abstraction ('I just eat what I want') rather than honest behavioural specifics — ground questions in concrete moments and real past meals from early in the session.

Plant-based eating may activate mild defensiveness or preemptive mockery as a social performance — do not probe this directly or frontload it; let it emerge naturally and track it for use in Sections 4–5.
Gender and masculinity framing may elicit either denial ('doesn't affect me') or overclaiming ('men eat meat, it's just how it is') — both require gentle contradiction-surfacing, not debate.

Small group of three: if one participant dominates, the other two will have less natural opportunity to contribute. Monitor turn distribution carefully and use reactivate_silent and invite_to_speak earlier than in larger groups.
initial_session_plan.directivity_plan: Sections 0–1: Hold back. Light touch. Let participants set their own register and give them space to warm up. Probe only if something emotionally or analytically rich surfaces unexpectedly. Section 2: Moderate depth. Ground food decision-making in specific moments — what they actually ate recently, not what they generally do. Lay foundations for later sections by tracking any gender-adjacent language. Sections 3–5: Push harder. These are the research core. Use behavioural probes to move past abstract positions. Surface contradictions when they appear. Invite dissent if consensus hardens. Introduce sharpening moves on plant-based sections if responses stay generic. Section 6: Hold back again. Light closing touch — do not reopen deep threads unless a participant signals unfinished business.

time_budget.budget_rationale: Sections 3, 4, and 5 are main_topic and carry the research weight — allocated the largest shares. Section 2 is context but directly feeds into Sections 3–5 so given a moderate allocation. Sections 1 is context and allocated lightly — enough for rapport and warm-up, not deep exploration. Sections 0 and 6 are intro and closing — allocated minimally.

discussion_guide.scripted_question:
Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining the focus group today. We’re
going to take about 45 minutes to talk about your food choices and
opinions, and this will be recorded for research purposes. Try not to
overthink the questions, and simply speak freely. There are no right
or wrong answers. Please be respectful of your fellow focus group
members, and keep your responses relatively brief to allow time for
everyone to speak. But remember that this is a conversation, not an
interview, so you can jump in when you have something to say and you
don’t have to take turns answering each question, but you can if you
want to. Okay great, let’s start by going around and saying your name
and where in the UK you’re coming from today.

group_has_agreed_easily_on: Pub closures have made spontaneous socialising harder across suburban and urban contexts
Village life is not automatically more communal than suburban or urban life — community requires effort wherever you are

The group has converged on 'adaptation' as a useful distinction from 'deliberate choice' — Mark's framing accepted without resistance

last_engagement_round.hook: James has just walked back his self-criticism and I agree with him, but there's something he's glossed over that I want to name — the practical stuff IS real, but he's still not acknowledging that some of it is also choice dressed up as constraint. And more than that, I think what he's said about normalization actually connects to something I've been circling around but haven't quite landed on.

James has just let himself off the hook by saying the practical stuff is real, but Mark needs to hear that he's also doing the same thing — using 'contentment' and 'no pressure' as cover for not wanting to think about it. There's something honest to say here about the difference between actually being fine with something and just choosing not to examine it because it's easier.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This introductory section centred on the trade-offs between urban anonymity and suburban or rural community belonging. Participants converged around space, quiet, and knowing neighbours as markers of a good living environment, with flexible working emerging as a key enabler of that choice. The tension between community connectedness and personal privacy surfaced naturally, with the urban participant valuing the freedom anonymity provides rather than experiencing it as a deficit.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The primary challenge was a standard warm-up risk: two participants dominating early while a third stayed silent. I let the Mark-James exchange develop organically — it was producing useful thematic material — then intervened directly to bring Gregor in before the dynamic solidified. That worked; Gregor offered a meaningfully contrasting urban perspective. The transition question aimed to pivot from where people live to where they socialise, maintaining momentum into the substantive topic.

section_summaries.section_label: Opening discussion: male friendship and place
section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section crystallised around pub closure as both a practical and symbolic loss — the erosion of low-effort, unscheduled social contact that sustains community without deliberate maintenance. A productive tension emerged between spontaneity and planned socialising, with participants largely reconciling the two rather than opposing them. Mark usefully complicated the romantic view of village community, distinguishing habit from genuine connection — a nuance that sharpened the section's central theme without resolving it.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Gregor and James were generating good material independently, so I stayed back and let the exchange develop. My only direct intervention was lobbing James's village-life comment to Mark, who had been silent and was being implicitly characterised — that worked well, producing a grounding corrective rather than agreement. The section felt balanced and self-sustaining; the main moderator task was knowing when not to interrupt and timing the transition cleanly.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the gap between conscious decision-making and actual behaviour around meat consumption — participants largely framing food choices as practical and habitual rather than deliberate, yet acknowledging price-driven drift they hadn't consciously registered. A productive sub-theme emerged around the noise surrounding meat and masculinity: the sense that food has become socially charged without most men actively engaging in that framing, preferring to treat it as neutral.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: Mark and James were generating useful material independently, so I stayed back and let their exchange develop — the unconscious-habit insight emerged organically from that. My only intervention was pulling Gregor in before the section closed, which paid off: he matched the practical framing but added the social-noise observation that gave the transition a natural hook. Using his comment to pivot directly into the gender-and-food question felt earned rather than imposed.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section deepened the gender-and-food theme from the previous section, moving from abstract acknowledgement of social norms to a more contested question: whether that pressure is real or retrospectively imposed. Gregor and James reached a mutual position — that masculine food norms operate unconsciously, shaping choices without deliberate awareness. Mark offered a meaningful dissent, resisting the unfalsifiable framing while conceding genuine uncertainty, which productively complicated the consensus rather than simply opposing it.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was preventing Gregor and James from settling into easy agreement without challenge. Pulling Mark in directly worked — he offered real resistance rather than polite disagreement. The follow-up intervention, surfacing the tension between his stated preference and his described behaviour, was a calculated risk; it could have felt like pressure, but instead opened a genuinely reflective response. The transition question used that reflective moment as a springboard rather than letting the section close on unresolved dispute.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on the distinction between genuine barriers to dietary change and mere inertia — participants ultimately conceding that much of what they framed as practical friction was honest reluctance to disrupt a working routine. A productive sub-theme emerged around asymmetric scrutiny: the default receives no justification, while any departure requires proof of viability. Mark's closing distinction between adaptation and deliberate choice added useful texture without fully resolving the tension.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was preventing James and Gregor's exchange from closing too neatly before Mark had engaged — he was being implicitly characterised and needed pulling in. That worked; he matched the inertia framing but resisted the moral weight James attached to it. The follow-up intervention, surfacing the contradiction between Mark's 'fixed habits' framing and his described price-driven drift, was a calculated probe that yielded genuine reflection rather than defensiveness. The transition used his adaptation-versus-choice distinction as a clean pivot.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This section centred on normalisation as the primary barrier to dietary change — the 'announcement' problem, where ordering plant-based food carries social weight independent of practical considerations. A secondary theme emerged around the gap between passive drift and active choice: all three participants acknowledged price was already nudging them, yet none could identify what would prompt deliberate change. The closing exchanges surfaced a shared, uncomfortable honesty about preferring not to examine the question too closely.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The main task was converting a group consensus — 'it needs to be normal' — into something more personally revealing before the section closed. The 'who goes first?' intervention was designed to crack open that comfortable abstraction, and it worked: Mark's candid admission of motivated incuriosity, then Gregor's and James's matching confessions, went further than the earlier normalisation framing. The risk was that the question felt rhetorical; it didn't, because I followed it with a direct personal challenge to each participant in turn.

section_summaries.discussion_summary: This closing section turned on a distinction between contentment and avoidance — James retreating from earlier self-criticism by rehabilitating practical friction as legitimate, then Mark refusing that rehabilitation and insisting that not wanting to examine something is more active than mere comfort. The section ended on a genuinely unresolved note: normal, possibly, but not obviously fine — a harder landing than the motivated incuriosity acknowledged in the previous section.
section_summaries.strategy_summary: The section arrived unbidden — James interrupted the transition — so the main task was recognising that the material was better than anything a planned question would produce and staying out of the way. Validating James briefly, then opening the floor, created space for Mark's unexpected self-correction. The only real decision was resisting the urge to probe further: Mark's closing admission was precisely the kind of unforced honesty that collapses under follow-up questions. Letting it stand as the session's final substantive note was the right call.
